The four dials, named from affine geometry

Hypercube Composition Theory. Homothety k, affine curvature κ, ℓp exponent p and cubic form C: one name per dial, each from affine geometry, with who found it and when.

DRAFT · The four dials, named from affine geometry

DRAFT, Nov 26 2026. Part of Hypercube Composition Theory (repo: fused-hyperoperation-algebra). Asked for by Brennan: rename the dials "now that we know them better, preferring their existing names", names that are "useful, not two people's last names", "from the language of shapes", "affine geometrical terms", with "a clear lineage" crediting the authors, and "a coherent system, not a Frankenstein monster". Builds on conics/ (section 4, affine curvature), simplex/ (section 7, the shape dial), shape-dial-survey/ (the three shape routes) and names-review/ (the circle operation ∘ₖ and the letter d). Checks: checks.py → checks_output.txt, 10 of 10 pass; checks_more.py (section 5 and the Δ reading) 23 of 23 (sympy exact where a closed form exists, numpy and scipy otherwise). Pictures: figures.py and figures_more.py → figures/.

The names

All four come from one place: affine geometry, as Blaschke organised it (geometry where straight lines and areas are kept, and lengths and angles are not). Three are standard objects of that theory; the fourth, p, has no name of its own there, and the table says so instead of forcing one.

The letters stay k, d, p and C (Brennan's choice, Nov 26). k and d are the two coefficients of one form, x² + kxy + dy², and they are the dials you turn. Curvature is not a separate dial: it is a reading of k and d, written with the form's discriminant Δ = k² − 4d. The curvature is −Δ/4 = d − k²/4, and the sign of Δ sorts the conics. No new letter is added, so nothing looks like k.

Old name New name Symbol What it does, in shapes Lineage (short)
k, the circle operation's dial (the "k dial") homothety (homothety rate) k ∘ₖ is doing one scaling and then another, all about one centre, the wall −1/k. k = 0 sends the centre to infinity, and scalings become slides (addition). Chasles (the word, 1827); Artin's dilatations (1957); Sugeno's λ (1974), Tsallis (1988), Coleman–McGuinness's c (1991), Borges and Nivanen–Le Méhauté–Wang's q-sum with k = 1 − q (2003–04)
plane dial d curvature dial (d keeps its letter; the curvature is a reading of k and d) d; curvature = −Δ/4 = d − k²/4, with the discriminant Δ = k² − 4d (curvature = d when k = 0) Each setting is one conic. Δ < 0 ellipse, Δ = 0 parabola, Δ > 0 hyperbola, smoothly through zero. Euler's affine curves (1748); Transon's affine normal (1841); Cayley (1859) and Klein (1871) for the measure; Blaschke (1923), conics are the curves of constant affine curvature; Coleman–McGuinness's d (1991)
roundness dial p ℓp exponent (no Blaschke name; see section 3) p Cross-polytope (p = 1) → ball (p = 2) → cube (p = ∞). Its departure from round is four-lobed. Lamé's curves (1818); Minkowski, a norm is a convex body (1896); Riesz's Lp spaces (1910); Blaschke's affine perimeter measures it (1923); Firey's p-sums (1962)
shape dial (round ↔ triangle) cubic form (Fubini–Pick form) C Zero exactly for ellipses; largest for the triangle. In the plane it can only make a three-lobed pattern. Țițeica's affine spheres (1908); Fubini and Pick (1910s); Maschke–Pick–Berwald theorem; Blaschke's apolarity (1923); Benzécri's shape space (1960); Calabi (1972); Cheng–Yau (1986); Loftin (2001), Labourie (2007)

Figure 1. The four dials, one picture each. Left to right: scalings about the wall; one conic for each curvature; the ℓp balls from cross-polytope to cube; a disk sliding to a triangle.

One sign convention, stated once. With ε² = kε − d (the repo's), d > 0 at k = 0 is the round side, like a sphere's 1/R², and Δ < 0 there. In general the round side is Δ < 0, the curvature −Δ/4 is positive, and the area-keeping unit squares to Δ/4 (so at k = 0, d = 1 it behaves like i, with i² = −1). Relativity is k = 0, d = −1/c². This matches Gauss curvature's sign. Tables that write i² = d (Yaglom's), and the Lean library's CliffordW with e² = κ, are the mirror of it.

What changes and what doesn't. Only words in the prose change. Lean names and code identifiers stay as they are (a comment maps them), so nothing breaks. The letter d stays in every formula where it already appears: it is Coleman and McGuinness's second number, and −Δ/4 = d − k²/4 is what it means geometrically.

1. k is the homothety

Figure 2. Left: the (k, d) plane. The lines of equal curvature −Δ/4 = d − k²/4 are parabolas; magenta is Δ = 0. Right: multiplying by the plane number ε is a scaling (the homothety part, k/2) plus an area-keeping turn (the curvature part).

  • The operation is composing scalings (H1). Let T_a scale the line by 1 + ka about the point −1/k: T_a(x) = (1 + ka)·x + a. Then doing T_b and then T_a is exactly T_(a ∘ₖ b). This is the repo's motion rule, and the wall −1/k is the scaling's centre, the one point that never moves. A scaling about a centre is what geometers call a homothety.
  • k = 0 is a slide (H2). When the centre runs off to infinity, a homothety becomes a translation, and ∘₀ is addition. Artin's name for the whole family, homotheties and translations together, is the dilatations.
  • Only k = 0 versus k ≠ 0 is a shape fact (H3). Rescaling the ruler, a → λa, turns ∘ₖ into ∘_(k/λ). So every k ≠ 0 is the same homothety law with a different ruler, which is why its size depends on what the page composes (weights, probabilities). The rule from the names review still holds: every page says what quantity it composes.
  • The same k in the plane (C1, C2). Multiplying by ε (with ε² = kε − d) has trace k and determinant d. Splitting off the scaling (k/2)·I leaves an area-keeping part ε₀ with ε₀² = Δ/4. So k is the homothety half of the plane law, and Δ (read with d) is the other half. Area grows at rate k under 1 + tε.

Why this name. "Homothety" says what k does in one word, in the language of shapes, and it is the word Chasles coined for exactly this: his 1827–28 paper is about homothetic conics. Known: all of it. Ours: using it as the dial's name, and the observation that the wall is the centre.

2. d is the curvature dial; the curvature is −Δ/4

  • Each setting is a conic (from conics/). The setting (k, d) is the conic x² + kxy + dy² = y, and its chord rule is our law.
  • Its curvature is −Δ/4 (C3). In equi-affine geometry (areas kept, lengths not), the conics are exactly the curves of constant curvature. For our conic it is 2^(4/3)·(−Δ/4), with Δ = k² − 4d, checked at six settings including both sides of zero. The 2^(4/3) is a fixed unit; only Δ moves.
  • Δ, not d alone, decides the type. The circle operation ∘ₖ sits at d = 0, but Δ = k² > 0: it is a hyperbola, not a parabola. Relativity (d = −1/c²) and the circle (d = 1) sit at k = 0, where the curvature is d itself.
  • Why no new letter. Δ is the form's own discriminant, the oldest name for this quantity, and its sign is the textbook test for ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. A separate curvature letter would sit next to k and look like it (Brennan noticed k and κ), and the Lean library already uses κ for other things.
  • It matches the other pages. The hypersphere page found the plane dial is "the sphere's 1/radius" and "1/R²". Those are curvatures; this pass says which one.

Why this name. The plane dial's job on every page is elliptic / parabolic / hyperbolic, which is the sign of a curvature, and affine curvature is the one that matches our law exactly. Section 5 gives an even cleaner reading: the centro-affine curvature of the unit circle |z| = 1 is −Δ/4 itself. Known: conics have constant affine curvature (Blaschke 1923; Nomizu and Sasaki 1994). Ours: that it equals −Δ/4 for our form.

3. p has no Blaschke name, and where it sits

Figure 3. Left: the only pattern a cubic form can make in the plane, three lobes. Middle: an ℓp ball departs from round with four lobes. Right: Blaschke's affine roundness of the ℓp ball, 1 at p = 2 and falling toward 0 at both ends. Orange dots are pairs p and p/(p − 1).

I looked for a true affine-geometry name for the roundness dial and did not find one. Here is where it sits instead.

  • It moves through the same space of shapes as the cubic form, but along the shapes with a centre of symmetry. A cubic form is odd, so it is zero at any centre of symmetry (P2). That is why the simplex page found every ℓp ball "round at the centre" and only the triangle not.
  • Its departure from round is four-lobed, never three (L3). The cubic form's is three-lobed (P1). So the two shape dials are different directions, not one dial twice.
  • Blaschke's own measure tracks it (L1). The affine isoperimetric ratio Ω³/(8π²·area) is 1 exactly at the ellipse (p = 2) and falls toward 0 at the cross-polytope and the cube, where all the affine perimeter has gone into corners.
  • A ball and its polar partner are not the same point (L2, a measurement). The ℓp ball and the ℓ(p/(p−1)) ball are polar to each other, but their affine roundness differs (0.869 versus 0.850 at p = 1.5 and 3). So the dial is not symmetric about p = 2 in affine terms, even where a law built on it is (Bell's 2^(1 + max(1/p, 1 − 1/p))).

Why this name. "ℓp exponent" is what every geometer and analyst already calls p, and it is how Minkowski's theory of convex bodies talks about these balls, so it is the existing name. Forcing a Blaschke word onto it would claim more than is true. If a one-word affine name is wanted later, the honest candidate is the measure, not the dial: affine perimeter.

4. The shape dial is the cubic form

  • Zero means ellipse. A surface whose cubic form vanishes is a quadric (the Maschke–Pick–Berwald theorem). On our dial that is the round end.
  • The triangle is the far end. The affine sphere over a triangle is Țițeica's surface xyz = 1, whose cubic form never vanishes, and which is as symmetric as a shape can be. The simplex page found the turn going from −1 (round) to 0 (triangle) along every route.
  • In the plane it is three-lobed (P1). Blaschke's apolarity condition makes the cubic form trace-free, and a trace-free cubic in two dimensions is A·cos 3θ + B·sin 3θ, nothing else. That is the same angular pattern optics calls trefoil (Zernike, 1934), so the optics name is a fair bridge for the picture, though the dial's name stays "cubic form".
  • Its space is Benzécri's. The dial runs through the space of convex shapes up to projective change; Cheng and Yau attach one affine sphere to each shape, and Loftin and Labourie read the shapes of whole surfaces off cubic forms.

Why this name. It is the standard name for exactly this quantity, and it pairs with the curvature −Δ/4: affine curvature and cubic form are the two basic invariants of an affine sphere. That pairing is the lead the conics page opened (plane dial + shape dial = the two invariants of one affine sphere), and these names now say it on their face. Known: all of it. Ours: reading the shape dial as this quantity (simplex page, section 7).

5. Other transformations from affine geometry

Brennan asked: "Are there any other transformations from affine geometry that we should incorporate?" Checks: checks_more.py → checks_more_output.txt, 23 of 23 pass.

Verdict. One adds something real: centro-affine geometry (maps that keep one point fixed). It gives the curvature −Δ/4 exactly, with no 2^(4/3), and it shows the curvature dial choosing between rotation, shear and squeeze. Projective geometry is too coarse to name a dial, because it treats every conic as the same, but it gives two good readings of Δ. The rest of the affine group is already in our dials.

Transformation What it is in our theory Adds something real?
Centro-affine (fix a centre, keep area) The unit circle of the plane numbers, |z|² = x² + kxy + dy² = 1, has centro-affine curvature exactly −Δ/4 at every (k, d) (CA1, CA2). Yes. A cleaner reading of the curvature than the chord conic's 2^(4/3)·(−Δ/4).
Rotation, shear, squeeze Multiplying by a unit plane number keeps area and turns: a rotation when Δ < 0, a shear when Δ = 0, a squeeze when Δ > 0 (CA3). Yes, as a unification. Shear and squeeze already appear across our notes; they are the curvature dial at zero and below. No new dial.
Equi-affine (keep area) ε = (k/2) + ε₀ splits each move into a scaling (rate k) and an area-keeping part (type set by Δ) (EQ1). Already on this page (Figure 2). It confirms the system: k is exactly the part that is not equi-affine.
Translation The homothety dial at k = 0 (H2). No, already there.
Dilation The homothety dial at k ≠ 0, about the wall (H1, CA4). The half-turn about the wall is the element a = −2/k (RF2). No, already there.
Reflection Conjugation z → z̄ (ε → k − ε) is a slanted mirror that keeps |z| (RF1). Small. Worth one line, not a dial.
Projective All conics are one conic projectively (PR3), so it cannot hold the curvature. It reads Δ's sign as how many points the conic has at infinity, 0, 1 or 2 (PR1), and the angle of a plane number as a logarithm of a cross-ratio, one formula for circular and hyperbolic angle (PR2). As a bridge, not a name. Goes in the lineage.

Figure 5. Left to right: the unit circles |z| = 1 for Δ < 0, = 0, > 0, with equal centro-affine arcs shaded; unit multiplication as rotation, shear and squeeze, every step keeping area; the chord conics with the plane squeezed into a disk, so the line at infinity is the dashed circle; conjugation as a slanted mirror.

  • Where the centre is. In the plane-number picture the centre is 0 and the identity is 1. On the line, the moves T_a(x) = (1 + ka)x + a fix the wall −1/k, not 0 (CA4), and in u = 1 + kx the law is plain multiplication. So the law is centro-affine about the wall; 0 is its identity, not its centre.
  • The centro-affine normal adds nothing. In centro-affine geometry the normal is the line to the centre, so it carries no information about the dial. The curvature is what matters.
  • What this changes. The curvature −Δ/4 is best read as the centro-affine curvature of the unit circle |z| = 1, with the chord conic's equi-affine curvature 2^(4/3)·(−Δ/4) as the second reading. The letters stay k and d. Rotation, shear and squeeze are the words for the three kinds of turn the curvature dial makes.

Known: centro-affine curvature, its formula det(z′, z″)/det(z, z′)³ and that central conics have constant centro-affine curvature (Olver's notes; Mayer and Myller 1933; Țițeica's centro-affine surfaces 1907); Laguerre's angle formula and the Cayley–Klein measure. Ours: that the constant equals −Δ/4 = d − k²/4 for the plane numbers' unit circle, and the table's matching of each transformation to a dial.

Lineage

Figure 4. Who found each idea, and when.

k, homothety. Michel Chasles coined homothétie; his "Mémoire sur les projections stéréographiques, et sur les coniques homothétiques" appeared in Gergonne's Annales, 1827–28. Emil Artin's Geometric Algebra (1957) groups homotheties and translations as the dilatations. The same one-parameter law reached us from four other directions: Sugeno's λ-measures (1974, A + B + λAB), Tsallis's entropy (1988, whose pseudo-additivity is this law), Coleman and McGuinness's rational formal group laws (1991, the letter c), and the q-sum x ⊕_q y = x + y + (1 − q)xy written as an operation by Borges (preprint 2003, Physica A 2004) and, independently, Nivanen, Le Méhauté and Wang (Rep. Math. Phys. 52, 2003). In that notation k = 1 − q.

d, the curvature dial (curvature −Δ/4). Euler (1748) named "affine" the curves related by transformations more general than similarities. Transon (1841) found the affine normal of a curve, the first result of affine differential geometry. Cayley (1859) and Klein (1871) built distance from a fixed conic, which is our ruler. Pick (around 1906) and Blaschke's school made the invariants systematic; Blaschke's Vorlesungen über Differentialgeometrie II: Affine Differentialgeometrie (1923) shows that constant affine curvature characterises the conics. Coleman and McGuinness (1991) gave the plane law the letter d. For the centro-affine reading (section 5): Țițeica's centro-affine surfaces (1907), Mayer and Myller on centro-affine plane curves (1933), Schirokow and Schirokow's Affine Differentialgeometrie (1962), and Olver's moving-frame notes, which give the curvature as det(z′, z″)/det(z, z′)³. For the projective reading: Laguerre's formula (1853), the angle as a logarithm of a cross-ratio, which Cayley (1859) and Klein (1871) made into a measure; Yaglom (1979) set out the nine plane geometries it gives.

p, ℓp exponent. Gabriel Lamé studied the curves |x|^p + |y|^p = 1 (1818). Hermann Minkowski's Geometrie der Zahlen (1896) showed that a norm and its unit ball are the same thing, which is why these are "ℓp balls". Frigyes Riesz introduced the Lp spaces (1910). Blaschke's affine perimeter (1923) is the affine measure of their roundness. William Firey's p-sums (1962) build ℓp balls from segments and start the Lp Brunn–Minkowski theory.

C, cubic form. Gheorghe Țițeica introduced affine spheres (Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo, 1908–09), including xyz = 1. The cubic form carries the names of Guido Fubini and Georg Pick (1910s); Maschke, Pick and Berwald proved that a vanishing cubic form means a quadric. Blaschke (1923) derived it, with the affine metric, from the affine normal and imposed apolarity. Jean-Paul Benzécri (1960) studied the space of convex shapes. Eugenio Calabi (1972, "Complete affine hyperspheres I") conjectured the picture that Shiu-Yuen Cheng and Shing-Tung Yau proved (1977, 1986). John Loftin (Amer. J. Math., 2001) and François Labourie (Pure Appl. Math. Q., 2007) parametrised convex projective surfaces by cubic differentials. Frits Zernike's trefoil (1934) is the optics bridge.

Letters, checked against the sources

Brennan asked whether we have two k's. Affine geometry has the same clash, which is why we add no curvature letter.

Dial Letter here What the sources write
homothety k k for a homothety's ratio (Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Wikipedia); ours is the rate, and the ratio is 1 + ka. Sugeno wrote this same law with λ.
curvature dial d, read as −Δ/4 k for the curvature of a plane curve, κ for the general-affine curvature (Encyclopedia of Mathematics); Olver writes κ for centro-affine curvature. Δ is the usual discriminant of a quadratic form.
ℓp exponent p p (Riesz, Minkowski); affine geometry has no letter of its own
cubic form C C in the Nomizu–Sasaki line (Nomizu–Pinkall); ψ in the Encyclopedia of Mathematics; the Pick invariant is J

The Lean library already uses κ in two other senses (the k dial in Behaviour, and e² = κ in CliffordW, the mirror sign). Those identifiers stay; the notes no longer use κ for a dial.

What this pass does not settle

  • The other dials (zoom, order, repetition, size, temperature, corner weights) were not asked about and keep their names.
  • The dates for Fubini and Pick are given as "1910s" because I did not reach their original papers.
  • I did not reach Laguerre's 1853 paper, Mayer–Myller (1933) or Țițeica's 1907 centro-affine paper; they are cited through Olver's notes and the papers below.
